lesson.text: Removing the name is not removing the person.

Data has two kinds of identifying power. Direct identifiers point at a person by themselves — a name, an ID number, a face. Quasi-identifiers seem harmless alone — a timestamp, a district, a coat — but in combination they can single a person out. De-identification fails not because names leak, but because combinations do.
THE CHAIN RULE — Any attribute shared between two datasets is a potential link. Sharding data into separate stores does nothing if the shards still share linkable values. Separation is not severance.

Picture a caravan that split its manifest into three separate ledgers, trusting that separation meant safety: a checkpoint log, a warehouse tally, a courier's delivery slip. No single ledger ever paired a crate with a name — yet a shared crate number and a shared hour let anyone walk the chain from checkpoint to warehouse to courier, and from courier to name. Each hop used a shared attribute; the chain gets there anyway. This is a linkage attack, and it is not theoretical: a famous study showed that ~87% of the US population is uniquely identifiable from just three quasi-identifiers — ZIP code, birth date, and sex. A researcher used exactly this chain, linking an "anonymized" hospital dataset to a public voter roll, to re-identify a state governor's medical records.

PSEUDONYMIZATION ≠ ANONYMIZATION. Replacing names with codes (Agent NIGHTINGALE, Manifest CR-822) is pseudonymization — reversible wherever a key or a chain exists, and still personal data under the law. Anonymization means no one, using reasonable means, can re-identify. It is a high bar, and most 'anonymized' datasets do not clear it.

One defense is k-anonymity: generalize (ages become ranges) and suppress (values become *) until every row is identical to at least k−1 others on its quasi-identifiers. Each person hides in a crowd of at least k. But the promise is only as strong as its weakest row — a single unique combination breaks it, and the mask slips for that one person entirely.

AUDIT RULE — k-anonymity is a property you VERIFY, not declare. Count the twins, every row, no exceptions — a dataset can look safe on average and still expose the one row with no twin at all. Declarations are not proofs.

And k-anonymity has limits even when perfect: if everyone in a group shares the same sensitive value, hiding in the crowd reveals it anyway (every crate in one shipment carrying the same contraband tells you everything without naming a single smuggler). Stronger tools exist — l-diversity, differential privacy — and they await at higher clearance. For now, carry these two lessons with you into the field: chains link, and masks slip.

quiz.q: A caravan's manifest code "CR-822" for a border crossing is best described as:
explain: Wrong — chaining it to a name de-anonymizes it. Nothing about the code was ever truly anonymous.
Correct — a code standing in for a person, reversible via the chain. Pseudonymized data remains personal data.
Wrong — the code names no one by itself; it only became identifying once chained to the other ledgers.

quiz.q: Which single change would have DEFEATED the linkage attack chaining a crate to its owner?
choices: Deleting names from the delivery slip too
explain: Correct — the attack needed one dataset that resolves to real identities. Remove the identity anchor and the chain ends in codes.
Wrong — renaming the ledgers leaves every link intact; the shared attributes are what matter, not the labels.
Wrong — adding more checkpoints leaves every link intact; the shared attributes are what matter, not the volume of data.

quiz.q: A dataset claims k=3. You find one row with exactly two identical twins and another row with none. The dataset satisfies:
explain: Wrong — k is set by the WORST row, not the best. A row with zero twins breaks any k>1 claim.
Wrong — the two-twin row would satisfy k=3, but the untwinned row still breaks the guarantee entirely.
Correct — k is set by the WORST row. A row with zero twins means at least one person is unique — the guarantee fails outright, whatever the average looks like.
quiz.hint: k-anonymity is only as strong as its WORST row — averaging or best-casing across the other rows doesn't rescue a guarantee that a single row can break.

variant.q: A guest log claims k=5. Eight rows have four identical twins each. One row has zero twins. The dataset satisfies:
explain: Wrong — k is set by the WORST row, not the best. A row with zero twins breaks any k>1 claim.
Wrong — the four-twin rows would satisfy k=4, but the untwinned row still breaks the guarantee entirely.
Correct — k is set by the WORST row. A row with zero twins means at least one person is unique — the guarantee fails outright, whatever the other eight rows look like.

quiz.q: Why is "87% identifiable from ZIP + birth date + sex" the same lesson as the caravan's crate-to-name chain?
choices: Harmless attributes combine into a fingerprint
explain: Wrong — the hospital study and the voter roll involve no smuggling at all; the parallel is structural, not situational.
Correct — no single attribute identifies; the combination does. Quasi-identifiers are judged together, never alone — on a caravan route, in a hospital, or a census.
Wrong — no hacking was involved in either case, just cross-referencing public or shared records.
